title: The view from above
hookLine: Marcus pictures the world from high up: herds of people, weddings, births, deaths (Meditations 9.30)

cards: You've probably had this happen on a plane. The wheels leave the runway, and in a minute the city you've rushed through all week turns into a map. The highway you sat in traffic on is a gray thread.
The office is a speck. Somewhere down there is your kitchen, and the argument you had in it this morning. For a moment, it all looks different.
Not unimportant. Just smaller, and somehow gentler. A Roman emperor practiced that feeling on purpose, with no plane, using only his imagination.
This week is about seeing life at its true size, and remembering we're mortal.

teach.b: Marcus Aurelius keeps coming back to an exercise in the Meditations. In George Long's translation, one passage begins: Look down from above on the countless herds of men and their countless solemnities.
Then he lists what he sees: the voyages in storm and calm, people being born, living together, dying.
Elsewhere he imagines the lives of people long ago: marrying, raising children, falling ill, feasting, flattering, plotting, all of it gone now.
The French historian Pierre Hadot, who spent his life studying ancient philosophy as a practice, gave this exercise its modern name: the view from above. Why would an emperor do this?
Partly to shrink his worries to their true size. From high enough, the insult at court and the delayed shipment look like what they are: small. Partly to shrink his pride.

teach.h: THE EMPEROR IS A SPECK TOO.
teach.b: From above, an emperor's palace is a speck too. But the third thing is the part people miss. The view from above isn't cold.
Marcus doesn't look down and sneer.
He sees everyone at once, doing the same human things: being born, marrying, working, grieving. From up there you can't tell the emperor from the baker.
It's hard to stay furious at one small figure when you can see how small and how human they all are, you included. So today's line has two halves. So small: the worry, the ego, the argument.
So loved: the people, each one living a whole life down there.

how: People who practice Stoicism often use the view from above, a guided imagining from Marcus Aurelius's Meditations, rising in the mind until their own worries and the whole human scene can be seen at once.

o: the historian who named the view from above
a French astronaut who saw Earth from orbit

games.q: what's inside the view — tap the pairs.
p: looked down on the countless herds of men
named it the view from above
the worry, the ego, the argument
the people, each living a whole life

s: the view from above is a way of looking down on people
Marcus doesn't sneer. from above, he sees everyone doing the same human things.
Marcus imagined the lives of people long ago, marrying, feasting and plotting
all of it gone now, and all of it human.
Marcus called the exercise the view from above
the modern name comes from the historian Pierre Hadot.

games.q: you're emperor of Rome, and someone at court has insulted you. you imagine rising high above the city. what do you see?
o: a speck of a palace among countless lives.
games.why: from high enough, the palace is a speck and the insult is small, and everyone down there is doing the same human things.

practice: Picture yourself where you're sitting, then rise slowly through the ceiling: your roof, your street, a neighbor walking a dog, then the whole town like a map, a mile below.
Somewhere down there is today's worry; notice its size, and all the lives around it. Then, slowly, come back down.

wordCard.voice: Hadot. The historian who named Marcus's exercise of picturing the world from high up, so worries shrink and people come into view. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: so small, so loved. The view from above takes you out of the traffic, so you can see the city. See you tomorrow.
